plan.title: Entropy: Why Energy Always Spreads Out
plan.description: Entropy measures how spread out energy is and how uncertain a system's state is. Learn the second law of thermodynamics and Shannon's information entropy in two minutes.

beats.narration: A hot coffee always cools down. It never heats itself back up. Why does time seem to run only one way? The answer is a idea called entropy.
Picture a drop of ink in water. It spreads until the whole glass is evenly tinted. It never gathers itself back into one drop.
Entropy measures how spread out energy is. Low entropy means energy is concentrated in a few places. High entropy means energy is dispersed evenly.
This is the second law of thermodynamics. The entropy of an isolated system left alone cannot decrease with time.

props.text: The entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease.

beats.narration: So isolated systems drift toward equilibrium, the state where entropy is highest. A consequence is that certain processes are irreversible, like the cooling coffee.

props.definition: The state an isolated system evolves toward, where entropy is highest and energy is spread evenly.

beats.narration: There is a second way to see it. Count the arrangements. Many microstates look the same from far away, and spread out states have far more of them.
A tidy deck is one special arrangement. A shuffled deck could be almost any of countless others. Systems drift toward the likely, and likely means high entropy.
In 1948, Claude Shannon used the same idea for communication. In his paper, entropy became the average uncertainty about a message's possible outcomes.
A coin flip with two equal outcomes is uncertain, so it carries one bit. A coin that always lands heads holds no surprise, so its entropy is zero.
So in physics, energy spreads out. In information, outcomes are uncertain. Both describe the same drift toward the likely. Next time coffee cools, you are watching entropy rise.
